newsitem.title: USA: YEAREND - Oilseed prices seen firm on tight supply.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - Oilseed prices seen firm on tight supply.

text.p: Oilseed prices should remain strong next year as world populations and bank accounts swell, increasing demand for meat and the livestock feeds and edible oils that are the main products of oilseed processing.
"The key point is the world does have a tight oilseed supply," said Mark Weidner, oilseeds analyst with Cargill Investor Services in Chicago.
"Increased population and increased GNP (gross national product) will keep demand growing. Price levels will not likely see any major breaks until we can ensure adequate supply," Weidner added.

Oilseeds are used to make protein supplements for livestock feeds and include soybeans, rapeseed and cottonseed. Soybeans alone account for more than half of world oilseed supplies and the United States is the leading producer.

While livestock feed is the primary use, oilseed products are also highly valued by industrial chemists. Oilseeds contribute to manufactured products as diverse as candy, baby formula, salad dressing, paints, adhesives and diesel fuel.

World oilseed production was expected to reach 255.3 million tonnes in the 1996-97 crop year ending next August, down from the previous year's output of 257.3 million tonnes, according to U.S. Agriculture Department data issued Dec 12.
The USDA projected world oilseed demand at 235.06 million tonnes. That would leave end-season stocks next year at 20.23 million tonnes, down from 22.25 million this year.

The tight supplies have underpinned oilseed prices for two years. From harvest lows of about $5.40 a bushel in October 1994, U.S. soybean futures were selling for about $6.40-70 a year later and rose above $8 a bushel before the 1996 harvest.
January delivery beans closed at $7.07 a bushel on Tuesday at the Chicago Board of Trade.

U.S. farmers produced about one-third of world oilseed supply this year. But with U.S. soybean production a fairly steady 65 million tonnes a year, analysts say all eyes will be on South America this winter as Brazil and Argentina tend to what are expected to become record crops by April.
Both South American producers in recent years have raised soybean plantings in an aggressive push for market share.
The USDA expects Brazil's soybean production to total about 26 million tonnes, second in world production and well above their five-year average of 21.63 million tonnes.
Argentine output is seen at 13 million tonnes, up from their 11.81 million tonnes for the five-year average.
Oilseed traders say South American weather remains the wild card, with any interruption in the growing season there likely to lead to sharp gains in world soybean prices.
"Because of the tight stocks and increasing demand, I think you have the potential for higher prices," said Mario Balletto, oilseeds analyst with Merrill Lynch Futures.
"The situation could become very volatile if problems develop with the South American crop," he said.
Some analysts say that even with the expected bumper crops from South America, given growing oilseed demand the added production would increase world supplies only slightly.

"The effect on world stockpiles will be minimal because there is such a shortage already," said Arnold Partner, Latin America division director for the American Soybean Association. "The carryout has been so low that we need to replenish the stocks," he said.
Many Pacific Rim nations are counting on bumper crops to provide cheaper supplies next spring.
Japan, China and other Asian countries have said they will buy from South America in the spring because those prices are expected to be lower than U.S. values.

And while Brazilian production was expected to reach record levels, domestic demand was also seen soaring. Brazil imported soybeans from the United States this year and was expected to buy more early next year.
"I would think that demand is probably going to be increasing the most out of southeast Asia and Central and South America," Balletto said.
One side issue to watch in 1997 will be crop genetics.
The European Union should continue to be the leading buyer of U.S. soybeans despite protests by environmental groups against certain genetically altered soybeans.
Europe was expected to account for about one-third of the United States' 24.5 million tonnes in soybean exports.
Protesters targeted U.S. crops grown from Monsanto Co's Roundup Ready soybeans that were genetically altered to be resistant to Monsanto's powerful Roundup herbicide.

Environmental groups like Greenpeace said the soybeans are a risky experiment with nature and might pose a threat to human health. But the crops have received a clean bill of health from U.S., European and Japanese authorities.
The protest groups demand that U.S. producers separate or label the new soybeans, but the USDA and grain industry counter that would be expensive and virtually impossible.

"With increased acreage in the United States and anticipated plantings in South America, there's no way that you can guarantee that you don't have Roundup Ready soybeans in any part of the world," Cargill's Weidner said.
